title: A transparent and generalizable deep-learning framework for genomic ancestry prediction.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Zenodo record 21133813 via its application programming interface: open access, CC-BY-4.0 licence, two files (Dietnet_training.tar.gz 263,231,609 bytes; Dietnet_inference.tar.gz 142,097,623 bytes). Both exceed our 50 MB download cap, so I used ranged requests to decompress each archive's opening bytes and list its leading entries: training holds config_rep1/rep3models.yaml, normalization_stats.npz (18,399,412 bytes) and SNPs_embedding.npz (662,359,940 bytes); inference holds DN_MODELS/snps_emb_model5.npz (132,472,196 bytes). I downloaded and parsed the authoritative label file (1000 Genomes Project sample panel, 55,156 bytes): exactly 2,504 rows, 6 columns, with 'pop' holding 26 population codes and 'super_pop' holding 5, and I printed the per-population counts. I read the GitHub README (10,487 bytes), which documents the genotype encoding and every pipeline script.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The training set of 2,322 individuals in 24 merged populations and 229,986 LD-pruned SNPs (single-letter DNA differences) on build GRCh38; the ShapeIT5 imputation and the 10%-missingness and monomorphic filters; the 5-fold by 3-repetition cross-validation giving 15 models; the 0.995 input-dropout setting retaining ~1,150 SNPs per sample; the PCA+random-forest and Rye baselines run on the same folds; and all CARTaGENE, Montreal Heart Institute and All of Us results. I never opened the prepared genotype HDF5 file itself, because it sits behind a 662 MB entry inside the 263 MB archive.

a1_downloadable.note: Zenodo, open access, CC-BY-4.0, no login: confirmed from the record metadata and by successfully range-reading both archives. Caveat recorded, not a failure: the three cohorts carrying the paper's generalization claim (CARTaGENE, Montreal Heart Institute Biobank, All of Us Controlled Tier v8) all need access applications.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The label is a plain column. I parsed the 1000 Genomes panel myself: column 'pop' gives one of 26 population codes for each of 2,504 people. The paper's 24-class target is that column after two documented merges (CEU+GBR, STU+ITU), and the recoded label file ships in the Zenodo training archive. Light recoding, not construction.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are the genotypes themselves, shipped as a prepared HDF5 matrix in the training archive (README documents create_dataset.py building it from a genotype file plus a label file). No per-sample identifier lookups. I did not open the HDF5: it is behind a 662 MB entry inside a 263 MB archive, over our cap.

a4_units_stated.note: Unambiguous. README states genotypes are allele counts with missing values encoded NA, ./. or -1; the authors ship per-fold means and standard deviations in normalization_stats.npz (18 MB, seen in the archive listing). The label is categorical.

a5_enough_rows.note: 2,322 labelled individuals across 24 classes, comfortably over the 400-row bar for classification. Flagged: features vastly outnumber samples (229,986 versus 2,322) and each class holds only ~97 people. The 2,322 is from the paper; the 2,504 it derives from I counted myself.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~0.5 GB as 8-bit integers, ~2.1 GB as 32-bit floats
a6_fits_laptop.note: 2,322 x 229,986 fits easily in 16 GB. The authors trained on an A100 graphics processor but also report running inference on 17,286 people using CPU only, so a frozen-embedding or PCA baseline needs no GPU. Total disk is several GB because the auxiliary SNP-embedding files are 662 MB plus 132 MB per model.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Reconciles exactly, and this is the strongest thing I verified. From my downloaded panel: CEU 99 + GBR 91 = 190 merged down to the paper's 107, and STU 102 + ITU 102 = 204 merged down to 105. 190+204-107-105 = 182, and 2,504 - 182 = 2,322, the paper's figure.

a8_label_provenance.note: 1000 Genomes population labels come from recruitment criteria, self-reported ancestry and grandparental birthplace, not from any model. Two caveats: the 26-to-24 merge was chosen because pairwise FST (a measure of genetic divergence between groups) was low, so the class definition was partly informed by the genotypes, making the task slightly easier by construction; and in the biobanks the authors excluded people whose RFMix v2 output disagreed with self-report, which would be circular, but those data are inaccessible anyway.

B1.why: Few files with clean keys: HDF5 matrix, fold-partition npz, normalization npz; saw the archive listing, not one table.

B2.why: HDF5 and npz need h5py/numpy and live inside a 263 MB tar.gz; the 55 KB label panel parsed first try.

B3.why: One assay only (1000 Genomes 30x sequencing); authors imputed missing calls and shipped per-fold normalization statistics.

B4.why: No censored values; SNPs above 10% missingness dropped and the rest imputed by the authors, per methods.

B5.why: No duplicates: related individuals removed by documented relatedness analysis, merged groups downsampled; my count arithmetic matched exactly.

B6.why: README documents every script, input file and genotype encoding; Zenodo description lists both archives' contents.

C1.why: Beating the published accuracy would fail; the leave-one-population-out reframing is descriptive since held-out groups have no true label.

C2.why: Saturated: Diet Networks, this paper's own released weights, Rye, PCA+random-forest and an XGBoost/Locator study are all open.

C3.why: Only a weak re-evaluation angle; the diversity angle lives in the inaccessible biobanks and 1KGP has no phenotypes.

C4.why: Already cheap and routine: PCA projection takes minutes, gnomAD ships a ready classifier, Rye runs at biobank scale.

C5.why: Published numbers on the identical folds: this paper's 15 models, its PCA+random-forest and Rye runs, plus Romero's 7.44% error.

D1.why: No DNA language model consumes a genome-wide dosage vector; only backbone that fits is the paper's own released ensemble.

D2.why: Released inference script already emits per-sample hidden-layer embeddings, and authors report CPU-only inference on 17,286 people.

D3.why: CC-BY-4.0 confirmed in the Zenodo record metadata; code on GitHub, permissive use.

E1.why: Leave-one-population-out and leave-one-superpopulation-out are available; the authors' own 5-fold split is random across individuals.

E2.why: 24 populations at roughly 97 people each, and 5 superpopulations; counted populations myself in the panel file.

E3.why: Majority class is about 107 of 2,322, roughly 4.6%; computed from the per-population counts I printed.

E4.why: No replicate genotyping or repeated ancestry labelling in this prepared set, so the noise floor is not estimable.

E5.why: Named in advance: recover continental separation, recover CEU-GBR near-identity, and predict sex from X/Y-linked SNPs.

E6.why: Label shuffling and random-SNP ablation both trivial; the authors' own input-dropout sweep is an ablation template.

E7.why: Open second sources exist (Human Origins 1,703 Asian individuals; HGDP 929 via gnomAD) but both are genomics-scale downloads.

E8.why: Authors shipped the exact fold splits and trained weights, so their accuracy and Romero's 7.44% error are reproducible.

G1.why: Standard but narrow keys: 1KGP sample identifiers and rsIDs/GRCh38 coordinates; sample IDs join only to other 1KGP products.

G2.why: Geuvadis has RNA sequencing on 462 of these exact individuals, joinable on sample ID; gnomAD joins on coordinates.

G3.why: Sample-ID join to Geuvadis is one-to-one but only 462 rows; coordinate join to gnomAD needs build and allele-flip care.

G4.why: Question is real (does the ancestry embedding beat superpopulation labels for expression variation?) but 462 people underpowers it.

H1.why: No 'unknown' class: every person must get one of 24 labels; out-of-reference individuals exist only in the inaccessible biobanks.

H2.why: 24 populations on 5 continents, but one project, one assay, ~97 per group, thin on Middle East, North Africa and Oceania.

H3.why: The honest claim is writable precisely in one sentence; see honest_claim_h3.

H4.why: Explicit in the paper: absence of North African training data, self-report limits and the 26-to-24 merge are all stated.

I1.why: Named: the Hussin lab in Montreal, CARTaGENE and All of Us analysts, and gnomAD's ancestry-assignment team.

I2.why: At most changes which ancestry tool a biobank analyst picks; they already use PCA projection or gnomAD's classifier.

I3.why: Analysts act at superpopulation level or on continuous admixture proportions, not on top-1 accuracy over 24 populations.

I4.why: The dumb thing works: the paper's own PCA+random-forest baseline is close, and Romero's PCA reached 9.33% error.

J1.why: Real grouped splits and frozen embeddings, but a low modelling ceiling and much genotype plumbing (PLINK, HDF5, builds).

J2.why: Population structure is easy to sanity-check with PCA plots, FST and known continental clusters; nonsense is visible.

J3.why: Useful at every stage: a clean 2,322-row feature/label table, then PCA baselines, then a generalization curve.

J4.why: No time budget definable while the cohorts carrying the interesting claim are behind access applications.

J5.why: No kill date written; nothing in the data or paper forces one.

existing_models.name: Diet Network (this paper's released ensemble of 15 PyTorch models)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on 2,322 individuals in 24 populations with 229,986 SNPs, using 5-fold cross-validation repeated 3 times; best setting was 0.995 input dropout, which held accuracy up to 99% simulated missing SNPs. Also evaluated on three external biobanks. The paper's exact accuracy value sits in Figure 1A, which I could not read from the text.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Populations absent from the training reference, named explicitly as North African: the model has no label for them and can only place them in a latent space, plus self-reported ethnicity in biobanks is a coarse stand-in for genetic ancestry.

existing_models.name: Diet Networks (Romero et al., ICLR 2017) - the original architecture, open code
existing_models.score_and_split: 7.44% +/- 0.45% mean misclassification error on 1000 Genomes ancestry, versus 9.33% +/- 1.24% for the best PCA result with 200 principal components; trained on 3,450 genotyped samples, i.e. more people than the 2,322 used here.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Features outnumbering training examples by orders of magnitude in genomic tasks, which is what the auxiliary network was built to mitigate.

existing_models.name: Rye
existing_models.score_and_split: Published in Nucleic Acids Research 2023; ancestry proportions from principal components, R-squared 0.998-1.00 against RFMix and ADMIXTURE for three-way admixed populations, and about 50x faster than ADMIXTURE on UK Biobank. This paper's authors ran it on the identical 2,322-individual, 229,986-SNP, 5-fold setup.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Reliance on well-chosen ancestral reference panels; accuracy depends on which reference populations are supplied.

existing_models.name: PCA + random forest (the gnomAD ancestry-loadings approach)
existing_models.score_and_split: Run by this paper's authors on the same 2,322 individuals, same 229,986 SNPs and the same 5 folds as the deep model; gnomAD publishes the loadings and classifier recipe openly.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Projection of new cohorts onto fixed loadings degrades when the query array covers the loading SNPs poorly.

existing_models.name: XGBoost / convolutional network / Locator comparison on ancestry-informative SNP panels (Human Genomics, 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: 95.6% accuracy and area under the curve 0.999 with 2,000 ancestry-informative SNPs on 1,703 individuals from 67 East and Southeast Asian groups (Human Origins data), using a random 80/20 train/test split - a weak split. Six algorithms compared; Locator predicted latitude and longitude.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Whether the selected ancestry-informative SNPs generalize beyond this dataset; Locator degrading in under-sampled or geographically heterogeneous regions; closely related populations overlapping genetically.

backbone.name: The paper's own released Diet Network ensemble (15 PyTorch models on Zenodo); no general DNA language model fits this input shape, since DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer, HyenaDNA and AlphaGenome all consume reference DNA sequence windows rather than one person's genome-wide variant dosage vector
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU: the released inference script already writes out final hidden-layer embeddings per sample, and the authors report CPU-only inference on 17,286 people
backbone.licence: CC-BY-4.0 (confirmed in the Zenodo record metadata); code on GitHub

integration.partner_dataset: Geuvadis RNA sequencing, which covers 462 of these exact 1000 Genomes individuals; secondarily gnomAD's ancestry principal-component loadings
integration.join_key: 1000 Genomes sample identifier (HG/NA accession) for Geuvadis; rsID plus GRCh38 coordinate for gnomAD
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a learned continuous ancestry representation explain individual gene-expression variation better than the coarse continental label analysts currently use as a covariate - a question neither dataset answers alone, but which only 462 overlapping people are available to answer.

controls.positive_control: Chosen in advance: the model must recover the textbook African / European / East Asian separation, must show the known near-identity of CEU and GBR (the low-FST pair the authors merged), and must nail sex predicted from X- and Y-linked SNPs as a trivially learnable target.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the 24 population labels and confirm collapse to the ~4.6% majority-class rate; replace genotypes with random SNP subsets of matched size; shuffle labels within superpopulation to check the grouped split really groups.
controls.external_validation: Open options exist but are genomics-scale downloads: Human Origins array data (1,703 modern individuals, 67 Asian groups) and the Human Genome Diversity Project (929 individuals, public via gnomAD). The paper's own external cohorts - CARTaGENE, Montreal Heart Institute Biobank and All of Us Controlled Tier - all need access applications.

honest_claim_h3: Among people who meet the recruitment criteria of one of 24 Thousand Genomes Project reference populations, genotyped at 229,986 LD-pruned common variants on genome build GRCh38, the model assigns the correct reference population most of the time; it claims nothing about admixed individuals or anyone from an unrepresented region, who must still be forced into one of the 24 labels.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a person's genome-wide genetic variants to predict which of 24 reference human populations they were recruited from.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is one person, represented by how many copies of a reference letter they carry at 229,986 common single-letter DNA differences (SNPs). There are 2,322 people, roughly 97 per population; I verified this reconciles exactly with the 2,504-person label panel I downloaded.
plain_idea.predict: One of 24 population labels. The true answer comes from 1000 Genomes Project recruitment records - self-reported ancestry plus, for some cohorts, where a person's grandparents were born - not from any laboratory measurement of DNA.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Biobank analysts need an ancestry label as a statistical covariate and the data is genuinely clean and reusable. But principal component analysis already does this job nearly as well, so the only thing we would really learn is how the model misbehaves on populations it never saw.

more_or_better_data.why: Our 2,322 individuals is smaller than what competitors used: the original Diet Networks trained on 3,450 samples, and the 2025 Human Genomics study used 1,703 individuals from 67 Asian groups out of the much larger Human Origins collection. We would hold less data, not more.

confidence_score.why: The released ensemble of 15 models already gives a per-person spread of softmax scores, and the paper already reports prediction variability across those 15 models for every biobank. The calibrated-confidence opening is taken.

models_beatable.why: The incumbent is this 2026 paper itself: weights, code and data released, 5-fold cross-validation repeated 3 times, compared against PCA+random-forest and Rye on the identical split, plus three independent external biobanks. That is honest evaluation, and recent.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No new data joins in cleanly. The obvious additions - Human Origins and the Human Genome Diversity Project - use different arrays, different SNP sets and different population-labelling schemes, so both the measured quantity and the evaluation split would change. The same-split and same-assay conditions fail.

label_elsewhere.sources: Human Genome Diversity Project (929 individuals, openly redistributed via gnomAD), Human Origins / Allen Ancient DNA Resource (used for the 1,703 Asian individuals in the 2025 Human Genomics paper I retrieved), HapMap, and the Simons Genome Diversity Project. All known resources; I verified only the 1000 Genomes panel myself.
label_elsewhere.join_key: Not a shared key across resources: each uses its own sample identifiers, so the join is by population code and genomic coordinate rather than by individual.
label_elsewhere.why: Population labels do exist for thousands of other people, which would make external validation possible in principle - but each source is a separate multi-gigabyte genotype release with its own population vocabulary, so it is small-and-hard-to-join rather than a ready-made benchmark.

ml_idea: The only version worth considering: use the authors' own released 2,322-person, 229,986-SNP matrix and their published fold splits to ask how ancestry classifiers behave on populations absent from training - hold out each of the 24 populations in turn, and measure where a held-out group lands and whether the distance between its latent representation and each training population tracks the FST genetic-divergence matrix. Freeze the released Diet Network ensemble, cache its hidden-layer embeddings on CPU, and compare against PCA plus multinomial logistic regression. This is cheap and cannot produce a useless answer, but it is also only descriptive, because a held-out population has no correct label to score against - and the authors already show the equivalent qualitatively for North African individuals in their biobanks.

effort.compute_note: Working set is arithmetic I did on verified dimensions: 2,322 x 229,986 is 0.53 GB as 8-bit integers and 2.1 GB as 32-bit floats. Embedding hours is scaled from the authors' statement that CPU-only inference ran on 17,286 people, so 2,322 across 15 models should be a couple of hours. The 10-minute figure is an estimate for one 5-fold PCA-plus-logistic run, not timed; retraining the Diet Network on CPU would be far longer than the 22 minutes they report on an A100 graphics processor.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Fit PCA plus multinomial logistic regression on the 2,322 x 229,986 matrix using the authors' own shipped fold splits. If it lands within about two accuracy points of the published deep-model number - and the paper's own PCA+random-forest baseline plus Romero's 9.33% PCA error both suggest it will - there is no headroom and the project is dead. One afternoon.

verdict_reason: The data is genuinely excellent and the question is not worth asking. Part A passes cleanly on checks I made in the files - the Zenodo record is open CC-BY-4.0, the label is a plain column in the 2,504-row 1000 Genomes panel I downloaded and parsed, and the paper's 2,322 figure reconciles exactly with it (two merged population pairs, 190 and 204 people, downsampled to 107 and 105, accounting for all 182 missing individuals). Part B scores 10/12. But Part C scores 4/10 and that is fatal: ancestry inference from SNPs is saturated with open, reproducible, honestly evaluated models (this paper's own released 15-model ensemble, the original Diet Networks at 7.44% error, Rye in Nucleic Acids Research 2023, gnomAD's PCA+random-forest, and a 2025 XGBoost study at 95.6%), and the existing method is already cheap - PCA projection takes minutes. Worse, I4 scores 0: the paper's own PCA baseline nearly matches its deep model, so a simple rule does the job. Part J fails at 5/10. Finally, the paper's one novel claim - generalization to diverse and unrepresented populations - rests entirely on CARTaGENE, the Montreal Heart Institute Biobank and All of Us Controlled Tier, all of which need access applications, so the interesting experiment is the one we cannot run.
